prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers to reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the configuration I reached after round 1: a single prize for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The discovery is the magic-wavelength lattice, in which the differential light shift cancels so that many atoms can be probed at once, together with the demonstration that this can be pushed to quantum-limited, many-body-controlled operation at 10^-18. It has been reproduced and intercompared by independent laboratories for over a decade, which is the maturity test I trust most, and it already tests relativity, constants and dark matter. The chair's summary shows the room splits four, three and one among B057, B015 and B053, and that nobody disputes that the clock is prize-worthy. I do not treat the count or the eight rankings as evidence. My reasons are that the physics is secure, the claim is a quantified measurement that others verify against their own clocks, and the attribution is the least distorted on the shortlist. I considered a two-part configuration, as the chair asked. Every pairing with B015 or B053 would force me to drop names from a three-person trio and break the Bistritzer-MacDonald-Jarillo-Herrero or Kane-Mele-Molenkamp chains, so I would rather defend one clean part than two damaged ones.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems is real, and the citation must not read as a prize for optical timekeeping in general. I would anchor it on the lattice concept and its realisation, not on records that others will surpass. The credit boundary is also a genuine exposure. Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock groups made decisive contributions to particular milestones, and a two-name citation leaves them out. I think the separable roles of Katori (concept and first lattice demonstration) and Ye (accuracy and many-body frontier) are defensible, but I cannot call the boundary clean. Finally, the clock is a discovery in measurement science, and it speaks less to the opening of a new regime of matter than B015 does. A reasonable colleague can weigh that more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B015 for the simple, checkable Bistritzer-MacDonald mechanism tied to a decisive experiment, ranks the clock seventh, and suggests waiting for the redefinition of the SI second.
responses.response: I find the B015 mechanism persuasive, and I take it as the strongest rival to my position. We differ on the standard. A continuum model that predicts a magic angle and an experiment that finds correlated phases is a real chain, but the superconducting mechanism is unsettled and the experimental credit leaves out Yuan Cao and the Dean group, whereas the clock claim is a number that other laboratories check against their own. On waiting, the redefinition is a decision of a metrological body that follows from the physics, so I do not think the committee should make the prize hostage to it. I do accept his request that the citation say what is new in principle, which is why I keep it on the magic-wavelength condition and the many-atom interrogation.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B015 first for opening a tunable platform that could not be seen before, applies an original-experiment test, and ranks the clock third as a compact and defensible pair.
responses.response: Her original-experiment test is a fair one, and the clock passes it for the concept. Katori's proposal and first strontium lattice demonstration are the original step, and Ye's accuracy and many-body work is a documented second one, so the credit follows two identifiable contributions. I agree that the moire platform opened more new physics, and that is why B015 stays on my alternatives. But I would not trade a confirmed, quantified advance for a younger platform whose pairing mechanism is open, and since she calls the clock pair defensible, I read our disagreement as one of ordering.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B053 first as a conceptual reclassification of electronic matter with a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp chain, and treats the clock as a possibly incremental continuation of earlier metrology.
responses.response: I respect the conceptual weight of topological insulators, and I have moved B053 into my alternatives because of it. I disagree that the clock is incremental. The magic-wavelength condition is a physics idea, and the many-body control of lattice gases at 10^-18 is a regime that neither the comb nor the ion clocks reached. My difficulty with B053 is the attribution he himself names: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Hasan's 3D branch and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal behind the HgTe experiment. I cannot judge that allocation well, as it is outside my field, so I weigh Mehlig's and Eriksson's disagreement over Mele and Hasan as a sign that it is unresolved.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B015 first, calls B057 the most broadly supported and cleanest attribution, defers to atomic physicists on the Ye contribution, and ranks circuit QED seventh because of the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept his reservation about B021 and the 2025 prize, and I have kept circuit QED out of my configuration for that reason and because of my own proximity to the field. On the Ye contribution, I can add what a quantum-optics theorist sees. Katori had the concept, but the demonstration that the lattice clock is a many-body system whose collisional and spin-orbit effects can be controlled, and then exploited, is what moved the clock to the 10^-18 level. I would resist the concern that clocks follow too closely on 2005 and 2012, because the lattice is a third thing and not a refinement of the ruler or of single ions. I agree that his B015 attribution questions, priority and the experimental co-leads, are not settled.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will read lattice clocks as a distinct achievement and not as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 optical-metrology prizes.
Whether Katori and Ye adequately cover the lattice-clock record given Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg, Ludlow and the strontium and ytterbium efforts.

Whether B015 will be judged ripe enough despite the unresolved pairing mechanism, and whether its credit survives the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto priority question and the omission of Yuan Cao.
I defer to colleagues on B015, B053 and B054, so my view of how settled their attribution is rests on their stated disagreements.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits, so I should recuse myself from any decision on B021 (circuit QED). I have not included it in my preferred configuration or alternatives. Kroll sits on the WACQT executive team, which the chair already flagged. I have no known tie to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or Hasan. My connection to the other shortlisted candidates is only that of a colleague in a neighbouring field.
